data.name: Distro_ubuntu_Description
data.value: Ubuntu is the most popular Linux distribution in the world, created to make Linux accessible to everyone. Based on Debian, it offers a polished GNOME desktop, broad hardware compatibility, and one of the largest support communities in the Linux ecosystem. It's the most common entry point for people migrating from Windows or macOS.

data.name: Distro_mint_Description
data.value: Linux Mint started out as a friendlier alternative to Ubuntu, focused on delivering an out-of-the-box experience with no extra setup required. Its Cinnamon desktop mirrors the layout of Windows (start menu, taskbar), easing the transition for new users. It ships with multimedia codecs and proprietary drivers pre-installed.

data.name: Distro_zorin_Description
data.value: Zorin OS was created by the Zorin brothers with the specific goal of easing the migration of Windows and macOS users to Linux. It lets you switch between interface layouts that mimic Windows, macOS, or Chrome OS, flattening the learning curve. Based on Ubuntu, it inherits its stability and hardware compatibility.

data.name: Distro_pop_Description
data.value: Pop!_OS is developed by System76, an American manufacturer of Linux-focused laptops and desktops. It's optimized for developers, content creators, and gamers, with excellent NVIDIA and AMD GPU support and an automatic tiling window manager (COSMIC). Based on Ubuntu, it keeps good compatibility with the existing software catalog.

data.name: Distro_fedora_Description
data.value: Fedora is sponsored by Red Hat (IBM) and acts as a showcase for the latest technologies in the Linux ecosystem — innovations like systemd and Wayland debuted on Fedora before reaching other distros. It strictly follows free software principles and has a release cycle of roughly 6 months.

data.name: Distro_fedora_Maintainer
data.value: Fedora Project (sponsored by Red Hat / IBM)

data.name: Distro_kubuntu_Description
data.value: Kubuntu is the official Ubuntu flavor that swaps GNOME for the KDE Plasma desktop, known for its high degree of visual customization — themes, effects, and window layouts are all adjustable. It keeps the same package base and repositories as Ubuntu, including Snap Store compatibility.

data.name: Distro_xubuntu_Description
data.value: Xubuntu uses the XFCE desktop, lightweight and low on resource usage, making it ideal for older or lower-spec computers. It's maintained by the Xubuntu community as part of the official Ubuntu family, inheriting the same repositories and package base.

data.name: Distro_manjaro_Description
data.value: Manjaro delivers the power and rolling-release model of Arch Linux with a simplified graphical installer and its own kernel and driver management tools. It's developed by Manjaro GmbH & Co. KG, with strong support from an international community of contributors.

data.name: Distro_arch_Description
data.value: Arch Linux follows the KISS ("Keep It Simple, Stupid") philosophy and a rolling-release model, always delivering the latest packages. It doesn't ship with a desktop environment pre-installed — the user builds the system piece by piece, aided by the renowned Arch Wiki, one of the most complete documentation resources in the whole Linux ecosystem.

data.name: Distro_arch_Maintainer
data.value: Arch Linux community (founded by Judd Vinet)

data.name: Distro_endeavour_Description
data.value: EndeavourOS launched in 2019 as the spiritual successor to the discontinued Antergos, aiming to offer Arch Linux with a guided installer while keeping the system as close as possible to vanilla Arch, without the heavy customizations of other derivatives. It's maintained by an international community of volunteers.

data.name: Distro_kali_Description
data.value: Kali Linux is developed and maintained by Offensive Security, a leading name in cybersecurity training. It's built for penetration testing, security auditing, and digital forensics, shipping with hundreds of specialized tools pre-installed, such as Nmap, Metasploit, and Wireshark.

data.name: Wizard_SecureBootBlockedMessage
data.value:
Secure Boot is enabled, and with it the firmware refuses to load the boot manager LinuxBit installs — the installation would stop at an error screen right after restarting.
To turn it off:
1. Open Settings > System > Recovery and click "Restart now" under Advanced startup. 2. Choose Troubleshoot > Advanced options > UEFI Firmware Settings and confirm the restart. 3. In the firmware, look for "Secure Boot" (usually under Security, Boot or Authentication) and set it to Disabled. 4. Save and exit (usually F10), let Windows start, and open LinuxBit again.
If the option is greyed out, set a firmware supervisor password first, or change the Secure Boot mode to "Setup Mode"/"Custom". Once Linux is installed you can turn Secure Boot back on.

data.name: Wizard_BitLockerBlockedMessage
data.value:
Drive {0}: is protected by BitLocker. To make room for the installation, LinuxBit has to shrink that drive — an operation on an encrypted volume that can fail or ask for the recovery key on the next Windows boot.
To turn it off:
1. Open Command Prompt or PowerShell as administrator. 2. Run: manage-bde -off {0}: 3. Track it with: manage-bde -status {0}: 4. Wait until it reads "Fully Decrypted" (this can take a while) and open LinuxBit again.
Note: suspending BitLocker is not enough — the data stays encrypted on disk. It has to be fully decrypted. Once Linux is installed you can turn BitLocker back on.
